intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene (139312) on chromosome 18p11.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia. It mainly affects the neck and usually begins in adulthood, although age at onset varies widely. The dystonia often spreads to other sites, especially the face, and can affect speech. Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that brachial onset was not seen and that arm involvement was less common than in DYT6.

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected. Their mean age at onset was 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7 affected members, the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) described 28 individuals with definite dystonia from 8 multiplex families with GNAL mutations. All were Caucasian of mixed European ancestry. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82%, and 93% had neck involvement at final examination. However, most patients progressed to other sites, and only 46% had focal dystonia at last examination. Cranial involvement was present in 57% and speech involvement in 44%. Brachial onset was not observed, and only 32% had arm involvement, which distinguished the disorder from DYT6. The authors summarized the phenotype as mainly cervical dystonia with a fairly broad range of age at onset. In over half of subjects the dystonia spread to other muscles, especially facial muscles. Some individuals had generalized dystonia with onset in the legs, and other onset sites included the larynx, jaw, and tongue.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in 2 families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia and found heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene in both. In family P they found a nonsense mutation (S293X), which lay within 1 of 3 regions of potential linkage (lod scores 1.5 to 2.1). In family D1 they found a missense mutation (V137M). The authors then Sanger sequenced the GNAL coding region in 39 additional multiplex primary torsion dystonia families of mixed European origin who did not have DYT1 or DYT6 mutations. This identified 6 additional novel mutations in 6 families (19%). The mutations segregated with disease in every family with DNA from multiple affected individuals. None of the variants was found in dbSNP135, in about 3,500 European exomes, or in 572 control chromosomes.

paragraphs.text: Family P had been reported previously and was of mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite heritage. Fuchs et al. (2013) found a heterozygous S293X mutation in affected members of this family. The mutation co-segregated with dystonia. In a BRET assay, the mutant protein failed to support any D1 dopamine receptor (D1R)-driven responses. In family D1, the heterozygous V137M mutation segregated with disease and affected a residue that is completely conserved in GNAL orthologs. In BRET assays, the V137M mutant showed an intermediate phenotype, which was largely consistent with impaired association with G-beta-gamma subunits.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) used a cell-based BRET assay in HEK293 cells. The assay measured G-alpha-olf function through its interaction with G-beta-gamma subunits during the cycle initiated by the D1 dopamine receptor. The S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses, and the E155K and V137M mutants showed intermediate impairment. A control variant, V16F, behaved like wildtype. The authors concluded that the assay results suggested loss of function. They proposed that GNAL mutations point to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission in striatal neurons as a possible cause of dystonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) studied 2 affected members of a family (family B) with primary torsion dystonia. They identified a heterozygous possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T-C; chr18:11,753,820, hg19) upstream of exon 4 of the GNAL gene. Bioinformatic analysis suggested that the wildtype sequence was 10 times more likely than the mutant sequence to be found near an acceptor splice site. However, the effect could not be proven because GNAL expression was undetectable in patient lymphoblasts.
